questions.stem: Thermoreceptors are:

options.label: A
options.text: activated only by severe cold or severe heat

options.label: B
options.text: located mainly in deep subcutaneous tissue

options.label: D
options.text: on dendritic endings of A delta fibres and C fibres

questions.why: Warm and cold receptors are free nerve endings of Aδ (cold) and C (warm) fibres in the superficial skin. They respond to ordinary, non-painful temperatures; damaging extremes are signalled by separate thermal nociceptors.

notes.A: They respond to ordinary, non-painful temperatures.
notes.B: They lie just under the skin surface.
notes.E: A, B and C are false.

questions.stem: The most significant heat source in the body is:
questions.why: The basal metabolic rate (cellular respiration) is the primary, continuous source of body heat.

notes.B: Conduction is a way of LOSING heat.
notes.C: Convection is a way of LOSING heat.
notes.D: Evaporation is a way of LOSING heat.
notes.E: Shivering is a reserve source, not the main continuous one.

questions.stem: A major means for conserving heat is:
questions.why: Cutaneous (skin) vasoconstriction reduces blood flow to the skin, conserving heat in the body core.

notes.A: Vasodilatation LOSES heat.
notes.B: This GENERATES heat; conserving it means reducing loss.

questions.stem: The thermoregulatory center is located in:
questions.why: The hypothalamus (specifically the preoptic area and posterior hypothalamus) is the primary thermoregulatory center.

notes.A: The cortex drives behaviour, not the thermostat.
notes.B: The vessels are effectors.
notes.C: The septal region belongs to the limbic system.

questions.stem: What is the normal body temperature?
questions.why: Normal oral body temperature is approximately 36.9°C (98.6°F).

notes.A: Not a body temperature.

questions.stem: At which temperature does the excitation of the thermoreceptors begin to cause pain?

options.label: A
options.text: at the temperature which causes tissue damage

questions.why: Temperatures above 45°C activate nociceptors (pain receptors), signaling potential tissue damage.

notes.A: Pain starts before visible tissue damage.
notes.C: 30°C is felt as cool, not painful.

questions.stem: Heat stroke is characteristically associated with:
questions.why: In heat stroke, thermoregulation fails. Sweating stops (dry skin), and the body temperature (BMR) skyrockets.

notes.A: Sweating STOPS in heat stroke.
notes.B: Raised metabolism is present, but dry skin is also characteristic.
notes.C: Hot dry skin is present, but so is raised metabolism.

questions.stem: As ambient temperature increases, heat loss increases by:
questions.why: When ambient temperature exceeds skin temperature, evaporation (sweating) becomes the only effective mechanism for heat loss.

notes.A: Radiation falls as the surroundings warm.
notes.B: Convection falls as the air warms.
notes.C: Conduction falls as the gradient narrows.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is produced by sebaceous glands?
questions.why: Sebaceous glands secrete sebum (an oily substance) to lubricate the skin.

notes.A: Adrenaline comes from the adrenal medulla.
notes.E: Mucus comes from goblet cells and mucous glands.

questions.stem: Following adaptation to a hot climate there is an increase in:

options.label: B
options.text: heat loss by radiation and convection

options.label: D
options.text: the ability to lose heat by sweating

options.label: E
options.text: decreasing arteriovenous shunting of blood to venous plexus near the surface of the skin

questions.why: Acclimatization to heat increases the capacity to sweat (earlier onset and higher volume).

notes.A: BMR tends to fall slightly with heat acclimatisation.
notes.B: These fall in hot surroundings.

questions.stem: Heat-loss mechanisms:

options.label: A
options.text: by radiation and convection increase when the ambient temperature decreases

options.label: B
options.text: by evaporation depend on sweat glands under sympathetic cholinergic (muscarinic) control

options.label: C
options.text: are controlled by the posterior hypothalamus

options.label: D
options.text: cause an increase in sympathetic tone to skin blood vessels

options.label: E
options.text: decrease arteriovenous shunting of blood to the venous plexus near the skin surface

questions.why: Sweat glands are innervated by sympathetic cholinergic (muscarinic) fibers, which stimulate sweating for evaporative heat loss.

notes.A: These FALL as the surroundings cool.
notes.C: The anterior hypothalamus controls heat loss.
notes.D: Heat loss REDUCES sympathetic tone to skin vessels.

questions.stem: The set-point temperature of the hypothalamus, triggering heat-loss or Heat-generating mechanisms is:
questions.why: The hypothalamic set-point is normally around 37°C.

notes.A: Too low.
notes.D: Lower than the usual set point.

questions.stem: When the temperature of environtment is above 34oC, the only heat-loss mechanism is:
questions.why: Evaporation (sweating) is the only heat loss mechanism that works when ambient temperature is higher than skin temperature.

notes.A: Above skin temperature, heat is GAINED by convection.
notes.B: Above skin temperature, heat is GAINED by radiation.

questions.stem: The set point level for body temperature is situated in:
questions.why: The thermostat (set point) sits in the preoptic area of the anterior hypothalamus, whose warm-sensitive neurons compare core temperature with the set point. The posterior hypothalamus organises the heat-conserving and heat-producing responses.

notes.B: The skin has receptors, not the set point.
notes.C: The spinal cord has receptors, not the set point.
notes.D: The posterior hypothalamus organises heat conservation and production.
notes.E: Brown fat is an effector (heat production).

questions.stem: The most potent mechanism for increasing heat production is:

options.label: A
options.text: activation of the parasympathetic nervous system

options.label: B
options.text: thyroid hormone increasing the metabolic rate

options.label: E
options.text: decrease in sympatetic tone to skin blood vessels

questions.why: Shivering thermogenesis can increase heat production by up to 5 times, making it the most potent short-term mechanism.

notes.A: It is the sympathetic system that raises heat production.
notes.B: Thyroid hormone acts slowly and less strongly.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a human thermoregulatory response controlled by cholinergic sympathetics?
questions.why: Sweat secretion is controlled by sympathetic cholinergic fibers (using acetylcholine, which is unusual for the sympathetic nervous system).

notes.A: Brown fat is driven by noradrenergic (β3) sympathetic fibres.
notes.B: Skin vessels are under noradrenergic control.

questions.stem: Capability to control body temperature is called:
questions.why: Thermoregulation is the process that maintains body temperature within certain boundaries.

notes.A: Osmoregulation controls water and solute balance.
notes.B: Thermodynamics is the physics of heat and energy.

questions.stem: The most important function of sweat is to remove from the body excess:
questions.why: Sweat evaporation is a crucial mechanism for dissipating excess body heat.

notes.B: Salt loss is a side effect.
notes.C: Water loss is the cost, not the purpose.
notes.D: Urea is removed by the kidney.

questions.stem: What is the result of a rise in body temperature?

options.label: A
options.text: decrease in the production of sweat

options.label: B
options.text: an increase in blood flow to the skin

options.label: C
options.text: narrowing of blood vessels in the skin

options.label: D
options.text: raising of hairs on the skin

questions.why: A rise in body temperature causes cutaneous vasodilation to increase heat loss by radiation and convection.

notes.A: Sweat production INCREASES.
notes.E: Shivering is a response to cold.

questions.stem: Which response to overcooling does not involve muscle contraction?
questions.why: Reduced sweating is a neural response that conserves heat, but it does not involve muscle contraction.

notes.A: Vascular smooth muscle contracts.
notes.B: Arrector pili muscles contract.
notes.E: Not a cold response, and breathing uses muscle.

questions.stem: What happens to the arterioles near the surface of the skin when the body temperature rises?

options.label: A
options.text: they absorb oxygen from the surrounding tissues

options.label: C
options.text: they move nearer the skin surface

options.label: D
options.text: they take in water from the surrounding tissues

questions.why: Arterioles near the skin surface dilate (vasodilation) to increase blood flow and release heat.

notes.A: Arterioles do not absorb oxygen.

questions.stem: Regarding the function of the cerebral hemispheres:

options.label: A
options.text: the parietal lobes are involved in pain perception

options.label: B
options.text: the frontal areas are involved in auditory perception

options.label: C
options.text: damage to the occipital lobes causes loss of hearing

options.label: D
options.text: the right parietal lobe is important for speech comprehension

questions.why: The parietal lobe (specifically the somatosensory cortex) processes pain and touch perception.

notes.B: Hearing is in the temporal lobes.
notes.C: Occipital damage affects vision, not hearing.
notes.D: Comprehension (Wernicke's area) is in the dominant, usually LEFT, temporal lobe.

questions.stem: Regarding speech:

options.label: A
options.text: in left-handed people the faculty of speech is mainly located in the right hemisphere

options.label: B
options.text: individuals affected by Broca's aphasia are able to speak only with difficulty

options.label: C
options.text: in right-handed people the faculty of speech is mainly located in the right hemisphere

options.label: D
options.text: an individual with Broca's aphasia will have paralysis of the lips and tongue

options.label: E
options.text: Wernicke's aphasia results from damage to the frontal speech area

questions.why: Broca's aphasia (motor aphasia) results in difficulty producing speech, though comprehension is intact.

notes.A: Most left-handers are still left-dominant for speech.

questions.stem: Regarding the electroencephalogram (EEG):

options.label: A
options.text: the normal EEG of an awake person is dominated by alpha waves

options.label: B
options.text: during deep sleep the EEG is always dominated by delta waves

options.label: C
options.text: the presence of theta waves in the EEG of an awake child is indicative of cerebral pathology

options.label: D
options.text: the EEG can be used to monitor the bioelectrical activity of the brain

questions.why: The EEG records the brain's electrical activity and is used to monitor brain function, sleep stages, and pathology.

notes.A: An alert awake EEG is beta; alpha needs relaxed, eyes closed.
notes.B: Deep sleep is not 'always' delta-dominated.

questions.stem: Regarding sleep:

options.label: A
options.text: reflects the intrinsic circadian rhythm of the brain

options.label: B
options.text: slow wave sleep is associated with rapid eye movements

options.label: C
options.text: young adults need less sleep than elderly individuals

options.label: D
options.text: during normal sleep the secretion of growth hormone is decreased

options.label: E
options.text: women need less sleep than men

questions.why: Sleep is heavily regulated by the brain's intrinsic circadian rhythms (controlled by the suprachiasmatic nucleus).

notes.B: Rapid eye movements occur in REM, not slow-wave sleep.
notes.D: GH secretion RISES in deep sleep.

questions.stem: The dorsal column of the spinal cord conveys the following sensations:
questions.why: The dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway carries fine touch, vibration, and proprioception.

notes.A: Pain travels in the spinothalamic tract.
notes.B: Temperature travels in the spinothalamic tract.
notes.C: Vibration is carried, but so is proprioception.
notes.D: Proprioception is carried, but so is vibration.

questions.stem: What regions of the brain are involved in emotional reactions?
questions.why: The limbic system (including the amygdala and hippocampus) and the hypothalamus are key centers for emotion.

notes.A: The hypothalamus is involved, but so is the limbic system.
notes.B: The cortex modulates but is not the core centre.
notes.D: The limbic system is involved, but so is the hypothalamus.

questions.stem: At what level the section of the spinal cord causes sudden death?
questions.why: A transection at the C1-C2 level paralyzes the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, causing immediate respiratory arrest and death.

notes.A: Below C3–C5, so the phrenic nerve is spared.
notes.C: Affects the legs and sacral function only.

questions.stem: Which are the functions of the brain stem?
questions.why: The brain stem (medulla, pons, midbrain) contains vital centers for respiration, cardiovascular control, and GI reflexes.

notes.A: Correct, but so are B and C.
notes.B: Correct, but so are A and C.
notes.C: Correct, but so are A and B.

questions.stem: The primary motor cortex, Broca's area, and the premotor area are located in which lobe?
questions.why: These motor and speech production areas are located in the frontal lobe.

notes.B: The parietal lobe is somatosensory.
notes.C: The temporal lobe handles hearing and memory.
notes.E: The prefrontal cortex is part of the frontal lobe but lies in front of these areas.

questions.stem: The medulla oblongata has centers for the following:
questions.why: The medulla contains vital autonomic centers (vasomotor, respiratory) and reflex centers for coughing, sneezing, and vomiting.

notes.A: True, but so are the other statements.
notes.B: True, but so are the other statements.
notes.C: True, but so are the other statements.
notes.D: True, but so are the other statements.

questions.stem: Lesions of which of the following nuclei cause hypothalamic obesity:
questions.why: The ventromedial nucleus of the hypothalamus is the 'satiety center'. Lesions cause hyperphagia and obesity.

notes.B: Not the satiety centre.
notes.E: This makes oxytocin, CRH and TRH.

questions.stem: Loss of fear and emotion is often observed in the lesion at:
questions.why: The amygdala is critical for processing fear and emotion. Bilateral lesions (Kluver-Bucy syndrome) cause loss of fear.

notes.A: Septal lesions cause rage and hyperemotionality.
notes.B: The thalamus is a sensory relay.
notes.D: Sensory cortex lesions cause sensory loss.
notes.E: Basal ganglia lesions cause movement disorders.

questions.stem: The Renshaw cells:

options.label: A
options.text: receive recurrent collaterals from motor neurons and inhibit other motor neurons in the vicinity

options.label: B
options.text: represent the inhibitory system of cerebellum

options.label: C
options.text: are a major component of muscle spindle

options.label: E
options.text: are present in the basal ganglia

questions.why: Renshaw cells are inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord that receive collaterals from alpha motor neurons and provide recurrent inhibition.

notes.B: Cerebellar inhibition uses Purkinje cells.

questions.stem: Premotor cortex refers to:

options.label: A
options.text: some areas anterior to primary motor cortex causing complex co- ordinate movements like speech, eye movements

options.label: B
options.text: an area of motor cortex responsible for voluntary movements

questions.why: The premotor cortex is located anterior to the primary motor cortex and plans complex, coordinated movements.

notes.B: That is the primary motor cortex.
notes.C: It is in the frontal lobe.

questions.stem: Functions of limbic system are all the following except:
questions.why: Vision is primarily processed in the occipital lobe, not the limbic system. The limbic system handles emotion, memory, olfaction, feeding, and sexual behavior.

notes.A: The limbic system began as the 'smell brain'.
notes.B: Taste links to limbic areas (insula, amygdala).
notes.C: The hypothalamus and amygdala drive feeding.

questions.stem: REM is:

options.label: A
options.text: characterised by delta waves on EEG

options.label: C
options.text: characterised by total lack of muscular activity

options.label: E
options.text: characterised by alfa waves on ECG

questions.why: REM sleep is called paradoxical sleep because the brain shows high-frequency, awake-like EEG patterns while the body is paralyzed.

notes.A: REM shows fast, low-voltage activity.
notes.B: REM is when vivid dreams occur.
notes.C: The eyes and diaphragm still move.
notes.E: The EEG shows beta-like waves, and ECG is not EEG.

questions.stem: Sleep deprivation:

options.label: D
options.text: has no effect on the individual

options.label: E
options.text: can cause reduction in arterial pressure

questions.why: Severe sleep deprivation can lead to profound psychological disturbances, including hallucinations and psychotic episodes.

notes.B: It SLOWS thinking.
notes.E: It tends to RAISE arterial pressure.

questions.stem: The naked nerve endings are responsible for the sensation of:
questions.why: Nociceptors (pain receptors) are free, naked nerve endings in the skin and tissues.

notes.B: Touch uses encapsulated receptors (Meissner, Pacinian).

questions.stem: In a healthy adult sitting with eyes closed the EEG rhythm registered with electrodes on the occipital lobes is:
questions.why: Alpha waves (8-13 Hz) are prominent in the occipital region when a person is awake and relaxed with eyes closed.

notes.B: Theta suggests drowsiness.
notes.D: Beta appears with the eyes open and attention.
notes.E: Not in a relaxed awake adult.

questions.stem: The basal ganglia are primarily concerned with:
questions.why: The basal ganglia are a group of nuclei involved in the regulation and coordination of voluntary movement.

notes.A: Sensory integration is cortical and thalamic.
notes.B: Short-term memory relies on the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex.

questions.stem: Lesions of which of the following hypothalamic nuclei cause loss of circadian rhythm:
questions.why: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) is the body's master circadian clock.

notes.A: Ventromedial lesions cause obesity.
notes.B: Dorsomedial is not the master clock.

questions.stem: Human circadian (24-hour) rhythms:

options.label: A
options.text: are triggered totally by external (exogenous) factors

options.label: B
options.text: depend more on the integrity of the cerebral cortex than of the hypothalamus

options.label: C
options.text: adapt within 48 hours on changing from day to night shift work

options.label: D
options.text: for melatonin secretion produce high night-time and low day-time levels of the hormone

options.label: E
options.text: for cortisol secretion produce peak values around midnight

questions.why: Melatonin secretion from the pineal gland peaks at night and is suppressed by light.

notes.A: They are mainly endogenous, set by light.
notes.B: The SCN of the hypothalamus is the clock.
notes.E: Cortisol peaks in the early MORNING.
